name: Marketing agency hero: headline text clipped to an inverted-color window of the background photo
notes: The signature move: two of the three headline words are set with background-image: the same hero photo, background-clip:text, then filter:invert(1) saturate(1.3) contrast(1.3) brightness(1.2) — so each letter reads as a bright inverted-color 'window' cut into the same dark photo behind it, no image editing required. Runs on city-lights-night.jpg (a starry night skyline with saturated red/teal/blue reflections) specifically because the color variety and the inverted starfield read as literal static/noise texture through the letters — a happy match with the 'Every Noise' headline that a plainer photo wouldn't give you; pick a similarly high-contrast, colorful night/light-source photo if swapping it out, not a flat daylight shot. Both image layers are pinned to the viewport rather than scrolling with the page — .hero-bg is position:fixed and .mask-heading span uses background-attachment:fixed — so they share the same viewport-relative crop at every scroll position and the masked letters keep reading as a true window into the photo (not two layers drifting out of registration) as the page scrolls past the hero. Verified by checking getComputedStyle(...).position/backgroundAttachment stay 'fixed' at scrollY 0 and 400+ on desktop. Both fall back to normal scroll (position:absolute / background-attachment:scroll) under 720px width AND under prefers-reduced-motion — iOS Safari handles a fixed background inside a scrolling page poorly (jitter, URL-bar resize glitches), and a strong pinned-parallax depth effect is exactly the kind of motion some vestibular-sensitive users want reduced. Keep the third line (.plain) as solid paper-white — an all-masked headline reads muddy; the contrast between one plain line and two masked lines is what sells the effect. Swap the background-image url in both .hero-bg and .mask-heading span together or the mask stops matching the base photo.
